props.title: RBG

sections.content: **RBG** (2018) masterfully chronicles Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's transformation from brilliant legal mind to cultural icon. Directors Julie Cohen and Betsy West craft an intimate portrait that goes beyond the "Notorious RBG" memes, revealing Ginsburg's methodical dismantling of gender discrimination through landmark cases. The film's strength lies in connecting her early ACLU victories to her powerful Supreme Court dissents. Like **On the Basis of Sex** (2018), which dramatizes Ginsburg's groundbreaking 1972 tax law case, RBG shows how strategic legal battles reshaped American society.

sections.content: RBG fits into a vital tradition of documentaries spotlighting pioneering women who challenged systemic inequality. **Miss Representation** (2011) examines media representation of women in positions of power, while **She's Beautiful When She's Angry** (2014) chronicles the birth of the women's movement from 1966-1971. These films connect individual struggles to broader social movements, showing how determined individuals catalyze institutional change.

The film's intimate access to Justice Ginsburg herself sets it apart. Unlike traditional biographical documentaries, RBG captures candid moments - from her legendary workout routine to her deep love of opera. This personal dimension enriches our understanding of her public impact, much like **Maya Angelou: And Still I Rise** (2016) reveals the woman behind the icon. The film's exploration of her 56-year marriage to Martin Ginsburg provides crucial context for understanding her life's work. SUBHEAD: Legal Pioneer to Cultural Icon

sections.content: RBG brilliantly traces how Ginsburg's careful legal strategy in the 1970s laid groundwork for later victories. Like **Marshall** (2017), which portrays Thurgood Marshall's early civil rights cases, RBG shows how systematic litigation can drive social change. The film's exploration of her evolution into a dissenting voice on an increasingly conservative court parallels themes in **The First Monday in May** (2016), examining how public figures can shape cultural conversations.
